title: How to answer gluten free questions on the phone
description: Answer gluten free questions on the phone by knowing what you can confirm, when to hand off to staff, and how to reply clearly.
question: How should I answer gluten free questions restaurant callers ask without slowing down the front counter?
answer: Answer gluten free questions restaurant callers ask with a clear script, a current menu, and a simple handoff rule for allergy-sensitive calls. You can confirm ingredients, prep notes, and sold-out items from your menu, but you should send serious allergy questions to staff with a summary. ROAL can answer menu, hours, and address questions, and hand tricky allergy-sensitive questions to your team.
summary: Learn a simple phone script and handoff process for gluten-free questions.
intro:
Gluten free questions restaurant callers ask should be answered clearly, quickly, and carefully. You can confirm what is on the menu, what modifiers are available, and when a question needs a staff handoff.

That matters because callers usually want one thing: can I order this safely, and what can I get instead? A clear phone process keeps the line moving and helps your team handle the tricky calls the right way.

sections.h2: What should I say when someone asks about gluten free options?
sections.body:
Start with a plain answer, then ask a follow-up question. The goal is to avoid guessing and to keep the caller from repeating themselves.

A simple script works well:

> "I can help with that. I can check the menu for gluten-free options, and if you have a serious allergy, I’ll get a staff member to confirm."

Use this order on the phone:

1. Ask what they want to order.
2. Check whether the menu already marks the item or modifier.
3. State what you can confirm from the menu.
4. If the caller says it is an allergy, send it to staff.

For example, if someone asks, "Is the grilled chicken sandwich gluten free?" you should not guess. A better response is: "I can check the ingredients and preparation notes, and if you have an allergy, I’ll have the kitchen confirm before we take the order."

If you use ROAL, it can answer menu questions from your public menu and hand allergy-sensitive questions to staff with a summary. That keeps the caller moving without putting pressure on your cashier during lunch rush.

sections.h2: How do I train staff and phone hosts to avoid bad guesses?
sections.body:
The biggest mistake is treating "gluten free" as one yes-or-no answer. In a real restaurant, the answer often depends on the item, the breading, the fryer, the sauce, the seasoning, and the prep area.

Make a short house rule for everyone who answers the phone:

- Never guess about a dish that is not clearly labeled.
- Never promise a fryer is gluten free unless the kitchen confirms it.
- Never say an item is safe for an allergy if you are not sure.
- If the caller says "allergy," send it to staff.

A practical script for staff is:

> "I want to be careful here. I can read what’s on the menu, but for an allergy question I’m going to have the kitchen confirm."

This works especially well for pizza shops, delis, and family restaurants where the same prep table handles many items. It is better to slow down for one call than to make a confusing promise.

ROAL is built to take the easy parts off your plate. It can answer menu, hours, address, and parking questions, and it can move allergy-sensitive calls to staff with a short summary. That means your team sees the important detail right away instead of starting from scratch.

sections.h2: What menu details should be ready before callers ask?
sections.body:
If you want gluten free questions restaurant callers ask to go smoothly, your menu has to be easy to read over the phone. The best setup is a menu that clearly shows which items are gluten free, which can be modified, and which need a staff check.

Make a simple checklist for each item:

- Main ingredients
- Sauces and dressings
- Bread, batter, or crust
- Shared fryer or shared grill notes
- Safe modifier options
- Sold-out items

For example, if a caller wants a salad, they may ask about croutons, dressings, or grilled chicken seasoning. If they want a burger, they may ask for a lettuce wrap instead of a bun. If they want pizza, they may ask whether the crust and toppings fit their needs.

A good phone answer sounds like this:

> "I see the salad on the menu. I can remove the croutons and check the dressing, but for an allergy I’ll have staff confirm before we place it."

This is one reason a clean, current menu matters so much. ROAL reads your public menu pages and can also use an uploaded menu, then answers from that live information. If your menu changes, update it once so callers get a better first answer. For more on making a phone-friendly menu, see [making your menu easy to order by phone](/blog/restaurant-menu-for-phone-orders).

sections.h2: How do I handle a real allergy call without slowing the line?
sections.body:
Treat allergy calls differently from general menu questions. The caller needs calm, precise help, and your staff needs the right summary.

Use this simple workflow:

1. Confirm whether the caller is asking about preference or allergy.
2. Read back the item they want.
3. Ask one clarifying question: "Is this an allergy or a diet preference?"
4. If it is an allergy, hand off to staff.
5. If it is a preference, answer from the menu and modifiers.

Here is a script you can use:

> "Thanks for telling me. Because this is an allergy question, I’m sending it to staff to confirm before we take the order."

That approach keeps your team from making unsafe promises and keeps the caller informed. It also helps during a rush, when one person at the counter cannot stop for a long back-and-forth.

A good handoff note should include:

| What staff should see | Example |
|---|---|
| Caller name | Maria |
| Phone number | 555-123-4567 |
| Item requested | Chicken wrap |
| Allergy concern | Gluten allergy |
| Notes | Caller wants confirmation before ordering |

ROAL already collects the caller’s name and phone, and it sends allergy-sensitive questions to staff with a summary. That makes the handoff cleaner and faster for your kitchen or manager.

sections.h2: What does this mean for pickup and delivery orders?
sections.body:
Gluten free questions do not stop at the menu. They affect pickup and delivery orders too, because the caller may want modifiers, notes, or confirmation before paying at pickup.

A good phone process for these orders is:

- Confirm the exact item.
- Confirm modifiers one by one.
- Read back any allergy note.
- Quote the ready time.
- Confirm the order back before sending it to the kitchen.

Example:

Say a customer wants a $28 order: one salad, one gluten-free pasta, and one soda. If you expect two similar calls in a day, that is $56 in sales. Plug in your own average order and your own call volume to see why clarity matters.

The key is not to overpromise. If the caller asks, "Can you make this completely gluten free?" do not say yes unless your staff has confirmed the full order and the prep steps. A better line is:

> "I can take the order and note the allergy, but I’m sending this to staff for confirmation before we finish."

That keeps the order process honest. It also fits how ROAL works: it does not take card numbers over the phone, it confirms the order back, and the ticket goes to the kitchen screen only after the order is completed.

sections.h2: How do I set up call forwarding and test it without drama?
sections.body:
If you want an AI phone host to answer gluten free questions restaurant callers ask, your forwarding setup has to work first. The codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call.

Common examples:

- Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off.
- On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off.
- On some carriers, **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in a web portal.

Before you go live, use this checklist:

- Confirm your forwarding code with your carrier.
- Test from a second phone.
- Check that the host hears your live menu correctly.
- Call after hours and during a busy moment.
- Make sure your staff knows how to turn forwarding off.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you can forward all calls or only unanswered and busy calls. That makes it easier to keep your restaurant number and still route calls where they belong. For setup details, see [how it works](/how-it-works) and [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should I tell guests when I can’t answer with certainty?
sections.body:
Honesty is better than a fast wrong answer. Guests usually appreciate a clear handoff more than a shaky promise.

Use short lines that feel helpful, not defensive:

- "I want to be careful with that one, so I’m checking with staff."
- "That item may depend on the sauce and prep, so I’m sending it over."
- "I can confirm what’s on the menu, and staff will confirm the allergy detail."

If you want a simple final rule, use this:

1. Answer what the menu clearly says.
2. Ask whether it is preference or allergy.
3. Hand off allergy-sensitive questions.
4. Confirm the caller’s name and phone.
5. Return to the call with a clear next step.

That keeps your front counter from getting stuck in long phone conversations, especially at lunch and dinner. It also protects your team from making a careless promise when the answer is not obvious.

takeaways: Answer the menu question first, then move allergy-sensitive calls to staff.
Never guess about gluten, shared fryers, sauces, or prep surfaces.
Keep your menu current so callers get a cleaner first answer.
Use a short script and a clear handoff note for serious allergy calls.
Test call forwarding before you send live restaurant calls to any phone host.

faq.q: How do I answer gluten free questions on the phone without guessing?
faq.a: Give the caller a clear menu-based answer, then hand off anything that depends on prep, fryer use, or allergy risk. A good line is, "I can confirm what the menu shows, and I’ll have staff check the allergy detail." That keeps the call moving and avoids making a promise you cannot verify.

faq.q: Should my staff say an item is gluten free if it can be modified?
faq.a: Only if your kitchen has already confirmed the exact version the caller wants. A modifier like no bun or no croutons may help, but it does not automatically make the whole order safe. It is better to say what can be changed and then route serious allergy questions to staff.

faq.q: What should I do if my menu changes a lot and callers keep asking about ingredients?
faq.a: Update the menu source your phone host uses, and keep a short internal note on items that need staff confirmation. If you use ROAL, it reads public menu pages and can also use an uploaded menu, so keeping that source current matters. That way your phone answers stay aligned with what you actually sell.
